prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: B006 remains the only candidate on which the committee has converged, and the round-1 exchange has strengthened rather than weakened the scientific case. Nobody has raised a maturity objection: the chain from proglucagon processing, to the insulinotropic truncated peptide, to human incretin physiology, to long-acting agonists with cardiovascular and renal benefit in large independent trials, is complete and still widening. The chair asked us to decide explicitly what the citation rewards. My answer is discovery of a principle: that GLP-1 is a physiological incretin, what its active form is, and what it does in the body. That is the Physiology or Medicine tradition, and the therapy is the proof that the principle matters. Drucker and Holst are the secure core, with Holst on human incretin physiology and Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology. I keep Mojsov as the third name because the identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide is the step that made the physiology testable and the drug concept possible. The citation names the therapeutic consequence so that the development line is acknowledged in the text.
statement.case_against: The third seat is still not settled on documentary evidence. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener and others is contested, and I have not verified it from primary documents. Habener is not among the credited names, so the real question is whether the record supports Mojsov's contribution on its own, not whether she outranks him. A discovery-only citation also leaves out Knudsen, whose acylation and half-life extension turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a drug, and that omission can fairly be called unjust. If the committee concludes that the record cannot support Mojsov, I would move to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation that names discovery and development, and I would not block it. I hold the Mojsov configuration only as the better-justified of two defensible options.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that the prize should honour the step that turned the physiology into a drug, that Knudsen's acylation and half-life extension is a scientific contribution and not only a commercial one, and that Mojsov's inclusion carries more attribution risk than Knudsen's.
responses.response: I accept that Knudsen's work is science, and I withdraw any suggestion that industry origin is itself disqualifying. Your attribution-risk argument is the strongest point against my configuration. But risk of dispute among academics is not the same as absence of merit, and I think the committee should not choose the third name by the risk of controversy alone. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide is a discovery that can be checked in the literature, and your own view is that a Drucker, Holst, Mojsov trio is defensible. My difference from you is therefore about what we are rewarding, not about whether the science is real. I would put the choice to the committee explicitly. If the majority wants the citation to cover development, I would join a Drucker, Holst, Knudsen award.

responses.point: The chair frames the choice between Mojsov and Knudsen as a decision on whether the citation rewards discovery or discovery plus development, notes that crediting an industry scientist breaks the usual pattern, and asks that it not be decided by default.
responses.response: I agree with your framing and have tried to answer it directly. My answer is discovery: physiology and active form of the hormone. I do not hold that industry credit is a matter of principle. Where a decisive contribution came from industry it can be recognised, but here the decisive scientific novelty is the hormone's physiology and identity, with half-life extension a rational engineering step on a known mechanism. I also take your point that your trio gives the more faithful account of what changed medicine. That is why my uncertainty is real, and why my fallback is your configuration if the priority record fails. I would not want us to reach it simply because Mojsov is harder to document.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved B006 ahead of B001, favours a discovery-focused citation, and argues that the priority dispute concerns who deserves the credit among academic scientists, not whether the peptide identification was necessary.
responses.response: That distinction matters to my reasoning, and it is the best argument for Mojsov: the dispute is over who gets credit for a step, not over whether the step was essential. I also agree with your point that the industry question should not be settled implicitly through the third name. Where I differ slightly is that I would not put the whole weight on the priority record. If the record shows that Mojsov's contribution was not independent, the discovery rationale for her seat weakens, and I would then prefer to switch openly to Knudsen than to keep her by tradition. On B001, your first-round case for a clean Feldmann and Maini credit is fair, and I have no objection to it as a later award. I would still not trade GLP-1 seats for it this year.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps Mojsov and would accept Knudsen only if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, and says Knudsen's engineering of a known mechanism is the kind of development the prize has usually left to clinical awards.
responses.response: I largely agree, and our positions are close. I would qualify one point: the prize has recognised development when it also revealed principle, and I do not want us to say that engineering of a known mechanism is by nature outside the remit. For this ballot the better argument is narrower: the physiology and identity of the hormone are the discovery, and the analogue is its application. Your fallback condition is the same as mine, that Knudsen enters if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended. I would add that the committee should decide that on the documentary record on GLP-1(7-36/37), and not on recollection, which none of us has verified.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record on who first identified the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) and (7-37) forms supports Mojsov's priority independently of Habener and others; I have not verified it from primary documents.
Whether the committee should make the citation explicitly discovery-only or discovery plus development, since this decides between Mojsov and Knudsen as the third name.
Whether a second prize part (B019 or B016) could be added without cutting the GLP-1 list below a fair credit, which I do not think is possible under the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections are a 2019 review with Grillner, collaborations with Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with committee member Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons; none involves a credited name. My neuroscience background is closest to B002 (optogenetics), which is not in my configuration or alternatives, so no recusal is needed. This is unchanged from round 1.
